newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- FEB 17.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- FEB 17.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--Foreign investors' confidence in the performance of the Athens Stock Exchange continues, with a new survey stressing that the rally has been led by Greek investors and that there are still underpriced opportunities on the ASE. Prices are reasonable, investors add, and the continuing fall of inflation and interest rates means the economy is on course for Maastricht.

--Fuel giant BP will challenge in the courts a a 41.5 billion drachma tax bill, reports say. The amount has been calculated on the basis of "oversights and mistakes" in tax declarations submitted in the 1988-92 period.

--Labour Minister Miltiades Papaioannou yesterday joined National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou in a joint statement of reassurance on the investment of pension fund reserves already deposited with the Bank of Greece in the secondary titles market.

--A new amendment to the government's plans for a 20 percent cpaital gains tax on buyouts of non-listed companies foresees tax being calculated on the age of the company, leading, finance ministry sources say, to a significant reduction in returns for the state. However, the amendment has been welcomed as an accurate reflection of the realities on the Greek market and will assist in the modernisation of older companies.

--The dramatic surge in prices on the Athens bourse since the beginning of the year is no flash in the plan: reliable sources at the stock exchange say that the conditions for a long-term upward course has been set, confirmed by projections of a 17 percent increase in profits for firms in 1997.
--Lower interest rates and competition between banks has been to the benefit of those seeking low-interest housing loans.

--The ancient pyramids concealed the curses of the EWgyptian pharaohs but modern-day pyramid investment schemes have also wreaked havoc on populations. In Albania, the situation has shown once again the risks involved; similar conditions exist in all Balkan countries which have neither the institutional or regulatory framework to prevent such occurrences. A way must be found to protect investors from political and social risks. Given Greece's stake in the development of Balkan economies, it is up to the state to give practical support to attempts by Greek businesses to penetrating these markets.

--The development ministry is putting the final touches to new laws defining relations between landlords and tenants in light of the deregulation of leases of over 12 years' duration later this year. Among the changes will be an increase in the value of commercial property and more difficult procedures to evict tenants.

--An agreement worked out between shop assistants and traders last week on opening hours has come in for criticism from the four major supermarket groups and appears ready to put the whole issue back on the drawing board.
--Belt-tightening at public utilities and organisations (DEKOs) on the cards under new and stricter guidelines which will include their submitting business plans with definite goals and checks.

--A snap amendment submitted by the government foresees all pension funds' reserve capital - estimated at around one trillion drachmas - transferred to the Bank of Greece for safekeeping. The move has caught both unions and fund administrators - as well as other ministers - by surprise and provoked an adverse reaction.

--Friday's decision by the Bank of the Greece to slash its overnight intervention rate to 11.90 percent pave the way for even speedier de-escalation of interest rates, due in part to the clear signals it gives of the BoG's confidence that inflation is heading downwards. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
